title: Alternative Legal Services Providers 2025: Strong Growth Amid Signs of a Bifurcating Market
author: Thomson Reuters Institute · Georgetown University Law Center on Ethics and the Legal Profession · Professional Service Firms Group at Saïd Business School University of Oxford

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s workflow-reconfiguration framing and materially extends it with survey evidence that GenAI is expected to streamline repetitive work, lower costs and reshape allocation between legal departments, law firms and ALSPs. It also supports selective delivery-model design and uneven organisational adoption, although its evidence is primarily forecast-based and does not directly assess verification or apprenticeship risks.
qs: Corporate law departments that expect to make more use of ALSPs think the technology will eventually enable ALSPs to streamline processes, handle repetitive tasks, and help provide cost savings.

To the broader question of which delivery model is best suited to a particular circumstance, corporate law department leaders should consider what goals they are looking to achieve — both at a matter level and more holistically — and which delivery models are likely to be most effective in which circumstances.

st.t: Operating model: AI shifts bargaining across providers
st.an: The source aligns with the cluster’s multi-provider operating-model thesis and materially extends it by identifying practical determinants of ALSP adoption: declining but persistent quality, confidentiality and data-storage concerns, existing familiarity with alternative delivery, and selection of delivery models around client objectives. Its GenAI evidence concerns firms’ plans rather than demonstrated returns or market-wide bargaining shifts.
qs: When asked about their concerns, answers were consistent with earlier research: quality, client confidentiality, and offshore storage of sensitive client information ranked highly; however, the percentage of respondents who cited these as barriers has mostly declined.

To the broader question of which delivery model is best suited to a particular circumstance, corporate law department leaders should consider what goals they are looking to achieve — both at a matter level and more holistically — and which delivery models are likely to be most effective in which circumstances.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The report aligns with selective, task-level deployment and materially extends the cluster with market evidence that corporate legal departments are disaggregating workflows and choosing providers matter by matter. It also locates ALSP advantage in bounded, scalable work while preserving traditional firms’ role in complex, relationship- and judgment-intensive matters; its GenAI claims are chiefly near-term predictions rather than demonstrated productivity outcomes.
qs: Over time, however, corporate law departments have become increasingly comfortable taking more discrete control over disaggregated matters and engaging ALSPs directly as part of matter workflows or even for entirely different lines of work.

ALSP leaders also said that when they are going after advisory work, it’s usually work of lower value and lower complexity — although they said they see a fit with high-stakes work, but not the most complex parts of it.

st.t: Workflow unbundling: Buyers challenge time-based production
st.an: The report directly supports the cluster’s core proposition that corporate legal departments are disaggregating matters and selecting delivery models task by task, with ALSPs concentrated in high-volume or less complex work while law firms retain capacity-, expertise- and judgment-intensive roles. It also supports coexistence and selective adaptation rather than wholesale substitution, though it provides little evidence on pricing reform, junior training or verification risks.
qs: Over time, however, corporate law departments have become increasingly comfortable taking more discrete control over disaggregated matters and engaging ALSPs directly as part of matter workflows or even for entirely different lines of work.

kp.k: Evidence combines 2024 surveys, interviews and 2023 market estimates
kp.d: The report draws on 424 law firm respondents and 213 corporate law department respondents surveyed from mid-September to mid-October 2024, plus interviews with 15 ALSP leaders and three corporate decision-makers. Market estimates use 2023 revenue data and multiple estimation techniques; spending and GenAI expectations are respondents’ predictions rather than observed outcomes.
qs: The 2025 Thomson Reuters Institute’s Alternative Legal Services Report presents the survey findings gathered from 424 law firm respondents and 213 corporate law department respondents, conducted from mid-September to mid-October 2024.
The report also includes findings from in-depth interviews with 15 ALSP leaders and three decision-makers within corporate law departments.
The market size estimates presented in this report reflect data from the year 2023.

kp.k: ALSP market growth substantially exceeds traditional legal services
kp.d: The report estimates a $28.5 billion ALSP market in 2023 and 18% compound annual growth from 2021 to 2023. This is slower than growth reported in the January 2023 edition but still faster than traditional legal services. These estimates describe ALSP market expansion, not a measured effect of GenAI.
qs: The result: we estimate a market size of $28.5 billion in 2023
and an 18% compound annual growth rate over the preceding two years.

While this growth is slower than that seen in our last report published in January 2023, it nonetheless shows that the ALSP market is growing much more quickly than the market for traditional legal services.

kp.k: Alternative delivery spans services without encompassing pure technology vendors
kp.d: The report replaces a law firm–ALSP dichotomy with a spectrum from licensed legal advice through consulting, flexible resourcing, managed services and matter-specific support to software. Its ALSP definition excludes pure technology companies, while acknowledging that ALSPs and some law firms sell software. Technology involvement varies substantially across these delivery models.
qs: While our definition of an ALSP continues to exclude pure technology companies, we have included reference to software products in this research in recognition of the fact that many ALSPs — and even some law firms — now sell software solutions directly to clients as part of their holistic offerings.
Those services closer to the software end of the spectrum rely much more heavily on technology as a core component of the delivery model.
Instead, they position themselves along a continuum of legal services.

kp.k: Corporate ALSP adoption combines direct purchasing and indirect delivery
kp.d: The survey reports that 57% of corporate law departments directly use affiliate and/or independent ALSPs, including 44% purchasing from independents and about one-third from affiliates. Law firms also incorporate ALSPs into client work, sometimes without explicit disclosure: 27% of corporate respondents believe their firms use affiliates and 28% believe they partner with independent ALSPs. These latter figures concern client beliefs, not independently verified arrangements.
qs: More than half of corporate law departments (57%) contract directly with ALSPs, according to respondents.
A sizable portion (44%) of corporate law department respondents said they have purchased legal services directly from independent ALSPs in the past 12 months.
In some instances, law firms will inform clients when work is being sent to an ALSP; in others, the firm is effectively white labeling the ALSP’s services.

kp.k: Existing adopters and nonusers show diverging sourcing intentions
kp.d: The report identifies an emerging bifurcation rather than uniform adoption. Among firms using independent ALSPs, 40% expect increased use and 1% a decrease; only 5% of nonusing firms plan to start in the next year. Figure 8 reports that 33% of corporate ALSP users predict reduced traditional-firm spending versus 12% predicting an increase, compared with 7% and 20% respectively among nonusers. These are intentions, not realized spending shifts.
qs: Some 35% of law firm respondents said their firms use independent ALSPs to deliver work to clients, and 40% of those said they expect to increase that use in the next year (compared to only 1% of those who predict a decrease in use).
Only 5% of respondents from these firms said they plan to start using ALSPs in the next year.
The only law department group that expects to spend more with traditional law firms are those who are not using ALSPs — which was less than half of the corporate respondents we surveyed.

kp.k: ALSPs both substitute for and complement law firms
kp.d: Corporate departments use ALSPs for cost-effective high-volume work formerly performed by firms and for capabilities such as legal operations consulting that most firms have not historically supplied. Interviewed law firm leaders acknowledge work displacement but generally characterize the displaced work as unattractive economically or strategically. The report also notes competition for finite client budgets, while finding ALSPs’ share of legal advice extremely limited.
qs: Corporate law departments are also tapping ALSPs for expertise that most traditional law firms have never offered, such as consulting on legal operations and tech-enabled delivery.
Further, law firm leaders are certainly aware that ALSPs are doing work that used to be done by law firms, but usually conclude that this work is not strategic or economically attractive.
And ALSPs have an extremely limited market share in legal advice — the most valuable and profitable service.

kp.k: Affiliate ownership correlates with broader alternative delivery adoption
kp.d: About one-third of responding firms have affiliates, with substantial size differences: 54% of large firms versus 12% of small firms. Firms with affiliates also use independent ALSPs more frequently—62%, compared with 23% without affiliates. Multiple-delivery firms offer a broader range of services, commonly using alternative divisions or partnerships for consulting, managed services and process technologies, while keeping flexible lawyers and paralegals more often within the core firm.
qs: These are more likely to be large law firms (54% of large firms say they have an affiliate, compared to 12% of small firms)
Among respondents from firms with affiliate ALSPs, 62% report that their firms also use independent ALSPs. That compares to 23% of those at firms without an affiliate.
Those that use multiple modes of delivery tend to be much more diversified, offering a wider spectrum of products and services.

kp.k: Expertise, profitability and flexible capacity motivate firm outsourcing
kp.d: Figure 19 identifies specialized expertise as the leading reason firms use third-party ALSPs, cited by 57%; competitiveness and greater outsourcing profitability each receive 38%, peak-demand capacity 37%, client cost control 36%, and technology access 32%. The report says technology access fell from second place in 2022 to sixth in 2023 and treats a shift toward software companies as conjecture; it notes that the 2022 question asked about specific work types.
qs: Access to specialized expertise 57%
More profitable to outsource 38%
In 2023, access to technology sank to sixth place, supporting the conjecture that some of that spending may have moved to software companies.
Respondents were asked to give reasons for using ALSPs for specific work types in 2022.

kp.k: Corporate sourcing retains strong in-house and traditional-firm roles
kp.d: Corporate respondents favor in-house delivery for cost, business familiarity and expertise, with about one-fifth defaulting to internal work unless expertise or bandwidth is lacking. Outside firms remain valued for specialist expertise, capacity and established relationships. Independent ALSPs have a perceived cost advantage, while affiliates have a small perceived advantage in speed and quality. The report does not present a simple replacement of firms by ALSPs.
qs: For about one-fifth of corporate law departments, the default is to keep work in-house, with outsourcing only being considered if the in-house team lacks requisite expertise or bandwidth.
When lacking the necessary capacity or expertise in-house, corporate law departments generally turn to law firms first.
However, independents have the edge when it comes to cost, and affiliates appear to have a small advantage in speed and the perceived quality of the work.

kp.k: Growth opportunities concentrate in existing relationships and managed services
kp.d: Among existing corporate buyers, 36% plan to spend more on legal managed services. Among current affiliate users, 41% anticipate increasing spending and 7% decreasing it. The Institute expects near-term opportunity in software-related services and expansion within already-converted clients, while interviewed leaders describe developing new services. These are prospective opportunities; the report also anticipates some software and advisory purchases moving to other provider types rather than independent ALSPs.
qs: legal managed services (where 36% of corporate legal buyers say they are planning to spend more)
41% of respondents from corporate law departments that currently are using affiliate ALSPs say they plan to increase spending with them, while just 7% predict a decrease.

The biggest short-term opportunity in the market likely lies in software-related services, where more respondents said they plan to make purchases and where existing clients are planning to spend more.
Indeed several ALSP leaders we interviewed described having a successful “land and expand” strategy.

kp.k: Confidentiality and quality remain significant adoption barriers
kp.d: Corporate confidentiality concerns increased to 44% from 26% two years earlier, while about half continued to cite quality as a barrier, broadly unchanged over six years. Law firm concerns include quality, confidentiality and offshore data storage, although the proportions citing them mostly declined. The report distinguishes perceived barriers from quality as a positive selection criterion, which fewer than 10% cite for any provider type.
qs: Some 44% of corporate law departments say they are concerned about confidentiality, which is up from just 26% two years ago.
And about half of corporate law departments cite quality as a barrier — a number that hasn’t changed significantly over the past six years.

Interestingly, less than 10% of respondents said that quality was a driving reason for using any specific type of provider, in spite of the fact that quality remains a significant barrier to ALSP usage.

kp.k: Affiliates plan expanded offerings, including licensed legal advice
kp.d: Among respondents at firms with, or planning, a nontraditional division, Figure 15 reports planned new offerings within 12 months: licensed legal advice 54%, consulting 48%, matter-specific services 45%, managed services 44%, and process and management tools 38%. The authors suggest that the legal-advice plans may signal differentiation on quality rather than just speed and price; this is an interpretation of plans, not evidence of completed launches.
qs: Law firm affiliates seem eager to satisfy that anticipated increase in spending, with plans to roll out a wide variety of services they don’t currently offer.
Chief among these is legal advice from licensed lawyers, perhaps showing that affiliates aim to continue to differentiate themselves on quality, rather than on just speed and price.
*Respondents at firms which have, or plan to create, a non-traditional division

kp.k: GenAI service development concentrates among firms with affiliates
kp.d: The report describes roughly one in six firms as actively planning GenAI-enabled offerings; Figure 21 gives 18% with active plans and 27% considering or exploring services over the next three years. Active development plans are reported by 40% of firms with affiliates versus 7% of traditional firms. Respondents anticipate streamlined processes, repetitive-task support and competitive advantage, while more cautious firms prefer to wait until technology is established.
qs: Among respondents from firms that have an affiliate, 40% said their firms are planning to develop services enabled by GenAI, compared to just 7% of respondents from traditional law firms who said that.

Given that the legal industry is typically cautious when adopting new technology, it’s notable that 45% of law firms are at least open to creating brand new GenAI-powered services to serve their clients.
In fact, law firm respondents said they anticipate that GenAI will help them develop more streamlined processes and become a resource for completing repetitive tasks.

kp.k: GenAI is expected to strengthen ALSPs near term
kp.d: The executive summary reports that 35% of law firm respondents and 40% of corporate respondents find GenAI-leading ALSPs more attractive. Figure 22 reports expectations of increased ALSP usage over three years among 44% of corporate respondents and 37% of firm respondents. Anticipated mechanisms include process streamlining, repetitive-task handling, cost savings and expanded offerings; these are survey expectations, not measured productivity gains.
qs: In the short term, 35% of law firm and 40% of corporate law department respondents surveyed for this report said they believe that ALSPs that are leaders in GenAI are more attractive, allowing those providers to better streamline processes, cut costs, and create competitive advantage.
In the next three years, many expect their use of ALSPs to increase as GenAI enables ALSPs to expand their service offerings.
Corporate law departments that expect to make more use of ALSPs think the technology will eventually enable ALSPs to streamline processes, handle repetitive tasks, and help provide cost savings.

kp.k: Internal GenAI capabilities could eventually reduce ALSP demand
kp.d: One-quarter of firm respondents and one-fifth of corporate respondents anticipate eventually needing ALSPs less because their own GenAI use could improve internal efficiency. The report emphasizes that few expect this near term and that the longer-term outlook remains unclear. Some respondents expecting declining use believe their internal GenAI adoption will outpace ALSPs’ adoption.
qs: One-quarter of law firm respondents and one-fifth of corporate legal department respondents said that at some point in the future, they expect to have less need for ALSPs mainly because GenAI will allow them to do work more efficiently themselves.
However, very few said they expect this to happen in the near term.
And those who are unsure or predict a decline in their ALSP use said they expect their own internal use of GenAI will outpace that of ALSPs.

kp.k: Institute recommends proactive client discussions and visible delivery innovation
kp.d: The Institute advises firms to discuss client objectives and appropriate delivery models rather than wait for explicit requests. Only 4% of firms without affiliates report client pressure to create one, versus 21% of corporate respondents encouraging firms to offer alternatives. It also recommends making affiliate contributions visible: 52% of respondents at firms with affiliates say clients do not work directly with the division, and 11% say clients are not proactively informed when work goes there. Its warning about traditional firms losing business is qualified by acknowledging that spending weakness may be transitory rather than structural.
qs: Only 4% of respondents from law firms without an affiliate said their clients are pressuring them to create one, but 21% of respondents from corporate law departments said they are encouraging their law firms without an affiliate to begin offering alternative legal services.
And 11% said that clients are not proactively made aware when the firm sends work to its affiliate.

Similarly, law firms would do well to initiate strategic conversations with clients to better understand their goals and how firms can support clients to best achieve those goals through appropriate delivery models.
However, this may be a transitory result rather than a structural one.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The report predicts that GenAI will strengthen ALSP offerings and near-term demand, while potentially reducing demand later as buyers become more capable of doing work themselves.
pts.d: The report attributes to surveyed law firms and corporate law departments the expectation that GenAI will streamline processes, handle repetitive tasks, reduce costs and support competitive advantage. Its executive summary reports that 35% of law firm respondents and 40% of corporate law department respondents consider GenAI-leading ALSPs more attractive. Figure 22 reports that, over the coming three years, 44% of corporate respondents and 37% of law firm respondents expect GenAI to increase their ALSP usage. Conversely, one-quarter of law firm respondents and one-fifth of corporate respondents anticipate eventually needing ALSPs less because of their own GenAI-enabled efficiency. Separately, the report describes plans for new GenAI-enabled law firm services: approximately one in six firms has active plans, with a substantial difference between firms with affiliates (40%) and traditional firms (7%). These are reported plans and expectations, rather than findings that the predicted efficiencies or demand changes have already occurred.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The AI claims principally rest on a 2024 survey of legal-market participants’ expectations and plans, not on measured AI performance or realized savings.
pts.d: The report surveys 424 law firm respondents and 213 corporate law department respondents from mid-September to mid-October 2024, supplemented by interviews with 15 ALSP leaders and three corporate law department decision-makers. The AI section explicitly attributes its predictions to survey respondents. Figure 22 separates significantly and moderately increased usage: respectively 9% and 35% for corporate respondents, and 9% and 28% for law firm respondents. Figure 21 shows 18% with active plans for new GenAI-enabled services and 27% considering or exploring them; the narrative summarizes this as 45% at least open to creating such services. No task benchmarks, quantified productivity tests or observed GenAI-driven cost reductions are presented. The report’s $28.5 billion ALSP market estimate and 18% growth rate concern 2023 revenues and 2021–2023 growth, respectively; they are market context, not evidence attributing growth to GenAI.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The report distinguishes a prospective three-year boost to ALSP usage from a less certain, undated possibility of later substitution by buyers’ internal GenAI capabilities.
pts.d: The three-year horizon is attached to questions answered in the September–October 2024 survey. Both new GenAI-enabled service plans and predicted changes in ALSP usage use this horizon. The later reduction in ALSP need is framed as occurring at an unspecified future point, and very few respondents expect it in the near term. Predicted benefits depend on providers implementing GenAI to expand offerings and improve delivery. The countervailing substitution scenario depends on law firms and corporate departments becoming more efficient internally; some law firm respondents expect their internal adoption to outpace ALSPs. The report also records caution among firms that wait for technology to become established, and explicitly characterizes GenAI as a source of unpredictability.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The predicted changes concern ALSP competitiveness, law firms’ service development and corporate legal departments’ sourcing decisions.
pts.d: ALSPs that lead in GenAI are expected to become more attractive to buyers through broader offerings and more efficient delivery, but may later face reduced demand if buyers internalize work. Law firms are both service innovators and ALSP buyers: those with affiliated ALSPs report substantially more GenAI service-development activity than traditional firms. Corporate legal departments anticipate cost savings and increased use of GenAI-enabled ALSPs, while some also foresee substituting their own improved internal capabilities for outsourced services. The report’s AI claims do not specify job losses, staffing ratios, changes to particular professional roles or access-to-justice effects. Its ALSP definition excludes pure technology vendors, although software sold as part of ALSP offerings is included in the research.
